771.title: A double portion (2 Kings 2:1–15)
771.hook: Elijah rises in a whirlwind; Elisha picks up his mantle
771.carry: an old cloak lying on the ground
771.howItsDone: Jews remember Elijah at the Passover seder with a cup poured for him, and the song Eliyahu HaNavi, asking for his return, is sung at the end of Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Naboth's vineyard, Elijah met the king with one question: hast thou killed, and taken? Today is Elijah's last day on earth, and someone won't leave his side.

Everyone seems to know what's about to happen. Elijah and his student Elisha are walking from Gilgal, and Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me to Beth-el. Elisha answers with an oath: as the Lord lives, I will not leave thee. At Beth-el, prophets come out and ask Elisha, do you know the Lord will take your master today? Yes, I know, he says. Hold your peace. Then Jericho: the same request, the same oath, another band of prophets, the same answer. Then the Jordan. Elisha will not be sent away.
screen: `STAY HERE.` → `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` → `HOLD YOUR PEACE.`

segments.voice: At the Jordan, Elijah rolls up his mantle, his rough prophet's cloak, and strikes the water. The river divides, and they cross on dry ground. Elijah turns: ask what I shall do for thee, before I am taken. And Elisha asks: "let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me." In Israel's inheritance law, the firstborn son received a double share, so some readers hear Elisha asking to be the heir. Some Jewish commentators also read it more literally, as twice his teacher's wonders. Elijah answers honestly: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it will be so; if not, it won't. As they walk and talk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha cries out: my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof. He tears his clothes in two. Grief first. Then he picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah, walks back to the Jordan, strikes the water with it and asks, where is the Lord, the God of Elijah? The water divides again. The prophets watching from Jericho say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. The inheritance doesn't arrive as a feeling. It arrives as an old cloak lying on the ground, and a river that still has to be crossed. And in Jewish tradition Elijah never quite leaves the story: tradition says he will return to announce redemption, and a cup is poured for him at the Passover seder.
screen: `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` · `THE FIRSTBORN'S SHARE.` · then, large: `A DOUBLE PORTION OF THY SPIRIT.` · then: `THE MANTLE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Recall someone who taught you, cared for you, or started something good and then moved on, or passed on, and name one piece of what they did that you admired: a way of welcoming people, a recipe. That's the mantle on the ground; picture picking it up. If you pray, you can remember them by name.
Pi shnayim. The Hebrew for a double portion, the share Elisha asked for as his teacher was taken. Today's word.
Your line: an old cloak lying on the ground. What a teacher leaves still has to be picked up. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: The Shunammite (2 Kings 4:8–37)
772.hook: a woman builds the prophet a room and asks nothing: "I dwell among mine own people"
772.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the Shunammite as a haftarah alongside the Torah reading of Abraham's welcome to his guests, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is honored as a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elisha asked for pi shnayim, and picked up an old cloak lying on the ground. Today he's on the road, and a woman in Shunem notices him.
screen: `AN OLD CLOAK LYING ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: A bed, a table, a stool and a lamp. The text lists them item by item. A woman in Shunem, called a great woman, has been inviting the traveling prophet Elisha to eat whenever he passes through. Then she goes further. She tells her husband: this is a holy man of God who keeps passing by. Let's build him a small room on the roof, with a bed, a table, a stool and a lamp, so he has a place to rest. No one asked her to.
screen: `A MEAL WHENEVER HE PASSES.` → `A SMALL ROOM ON THE ROOF.` → `A BED, A TABLE, A STOOL, A LAMP.`

segments.voice: One day, resting in that room, Elisha wants to repay her. He sends his servant Gehazi with an offer: you've taken all this trouble for us; what can be done for you? Shall we speak for you to the king, or to the captain of the army? It's a real offer; a prophet's word in the right ear could open doors. Her answer is quiet and complete: "I dwell among mine own people." Her hospitality wasn't an investment. Elisha doesn't let it go. Gehazi points out that she has no son, and her husband is old. So Elisha tells her: about this season next year, you will hold a son. Her reply is startling: no, my lord, do not lie to your handmaid. She had never asked for it. And the son is born. When the child has grown, he goes out to his father in the field and cries, my head, my head. He is carried to his mother, and dies on her lap. She lays him on the prophet's bed in the little room, shuts the door, and rides straight to find Elisha. Asked on the way whether all is well, she says only: it is well. Then at Elisha's feet the grief pours out. Elisha comes, prays, stretches himself over the child, and the boy sneezes and opens his eyes. And look where the miracle happens: in the room she built for a stranger. The space she made out of kindness, asking nothing, became the place where her son was given back to her.

773.title: Wash, and be clean (2 Kings 5:1–14)
773.hook: the general wanted something grand, and was told to wash in the Jordan
773.howItsDone: Jews read Naaman's healing as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws of skin disease, which are read in the book of Leviticus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shunammite made room for a stranger and asked nothing back: I dwell among my people. Today, someone pulls up at Elisha's door with horses and chariots.

Horses, chariots, servants, and gifts of silver, gold and fine clothing. Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Aram, has come a long way, and he has come in style. The text calls him a great man, honored by his king, a mighty man of valor. And then a short phrase undoes all of it: he was a leper. He has a skin disease no rank can cure. Someone has told him there's a prophet in Israel who could heal him. So the whole procession stops at Elisha's door. And Elisha doesn't come out.
screen: `HORSES, CHARIOTS, SILVER, GOLD.` → `A GREAT MAN, BUT A LEPER.` → `ELISHA DOESN'T COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Instead, Elisha sends a messenger: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean. No ceremony. No prophet at the door. Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear why. I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of his God, wave his hand over the spot, and heal me. He had pictured the whole scene in advance. Then the insult of the river itself: are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean? He turns and leaves in a rage. What stops him is not the prophet. It's his own servants. They call him, my father. If the prophet had asked you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? "How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" A sharp, kind question. Naaman was ready for a quest, a price, a drama worthy of a general. What he couldn't accept was something ordinary: a plain river, seven dips, no prophet at the bank. And yet he goes down to the Jordan, dips himself seven times, just as the man of God said, and his flesh comes back like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean. The cure was there from the first message. What stood in the way was Naaman's picture of how it should happen. The hard part wasn't the washing. It was getting down off the chariot.
screen: `GO AND WASH IN THE JORDAN.` · `I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.` · then, large: `WASH, AND BE CLEAN.` · then: `LIKE THE FLESH OF A LITTLE CHILD.`

Ask what Naaman's servants asked: if the answer were something grand, would I do it, and what's the plain, ordinary step I keep stepping over? Name it to yourself, and in your mind, step down off the chariot.

774.title: The captive girl (2 Kings 5:2–3)
774.hook: an Israelite servant girl points her master toward healing
774.howItsDone: Jews read the captive girl's words at the start of Naaman's story in the book of Kings, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great general almost refused the plain instruction: getting down off the chariot. Today we go back to the person who sent him to the prophet at all.

She gets only a few lines. No name, no age, no words about her family. Raiding bands from Aram had gone into the land of Israel, and among what they carried off was a young girl. Now she works in a foreign house, waiting on the wife of the commander whose raiders took her. That commander is Naaman. Everything we heard yesterday, the chariots, the gifts, the river, begins with something this girl says to her mistress.
screen: `A FEW LINES, NO NAME.` → `CARRIED OFF BY RAIDERS.` → `SERVING IN NAAMAN'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." Look at who she's talking about. My lord. The man whose soldiers took her from her home. And her wish is for him to be healed. The text doesn't tell us what she felt, whether she was afraid, or homesick, or angry. It doesn't explain her motives at all. It only gives us the sentence, and the sentence is generous. Then watch how far it travels. Word goes up the household: thus and thus said the maid from the land of Israel. It reaches the king of Aram, and he writes a letter to the king of Israel. Armies, kings and letters start moving, all because a servant girl spoke up. The king of Israel panics when he reads it, tearing his clothes: am I God, to kill and to make alive? The king doesn't think of the prophet. The girl did. She knew there was a prophet in Samaria, and she trusted he could help. Two more things stand out. She points away from herself; she claims no power, she simply knows where help can be found. And the story never mentions her again. No reward, no freedom, no thanks recorded. Naaman comes home healed, and the text has already moved on. But the healing began with one sentence from someone with no power at all, and the text bothered to keep it.
screen: `WOULD GOD MY LORD WERE WITH THE PROPHET.` · `THE SENTENCE TRAVELS TO KINGS.` · then, large: `A SMALL GIRL'S WORD.` · then: `NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: This one is hard, so go gently: think of someone who hurt you in a small or middle-sized way, not the deepest wound, and without excusing what they did, ask the girl's question: is there one good thing I could wish for this person? Healing, rest, a better day; let the wish sit for a few breaths, and if it won't come, that's honest too. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers.
Na'arah ketanah. Hebrew for "a little maid," how the text describes a young Israelite taken by raiders, serving in Naaman's house, whose one sentence sent her master to be healed. Today's word.
Your line: a small girl's word. The smallest voice in the house knew where help was. See you tomorrow.

775.title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
775.hook: Elisha prays his servant will see the unseen help around them
775.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Elisha at Dothan as part of the book of Kings; Elisha's line that those with us are more than those with them is remembered as words of courage in frightening times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, na'arah ketanah, a captive girl with no name, spoke one generous sentence that set kings in motion: a small girl's word. Today, Elisha's servant wakes up early and looks outside.

Dawn in the town of Dothan. The servant of Elisha gets up early, steps out, and stops. An army has surrounded the city in the night: horses, chariots, a great host. The king of Aram has been at war with Israel, and not once nor twice, the text says, Elisha has warned the king of Israel where the ambush is. So the king of Aram has sent a whole army to capture one prophet. The servant runs back inside, in pure panic: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?"
screen: `DAWN IN DOTHAN.` → `AN ARMY AROUND THE CITY.` → `ALAS, MY MASTER!`

segments.voice: Elisha's answer is calm, and at first it sounds impossible: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." More? The servant can see an army outside, and on his side, one prophet. Elisha doesn't argue or explain. He prays one short line: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." He doesn't ask for the army to disappear, or for rescue, or for fire from heaven. He asks for his servant to see. And the Lord opened the young man's eyes, "and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha." The help had been there the whole time. Nothing outside changed; the servant did. Not long before, a chariot of fire parted Elijah from his student. Now chariots of fire surround that student, and Elisha knew it before anyone saw them. Then a surprising turn. Elisha prays that the enemy soldiers be struck with blindness, and leads them, confused, right into Samaria, to the king of Israel. Shall I strike them? the king asks. Elisha says no: set bread and water before them, let them eat and drink, and send them home. And the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel. So the chapter is about two kinds of sight. The servant learns to see help he couldn't see. Israel's king is asked to see enemies as hungry men who could be fed. In both, the first change happens in someone's eyes.
screen: `MORE ARE WITH US.` · `NOT RESCUE: SIGHT.` · then, large: `OPEN HIS EYES.` · then: `BREAD FOR THE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: Start with whatever feels like an army around your city today, a deadline, a worry, a stretch of loneliness, and feel how big it is. Then, like the servant, look again at what's already around you: the chair holding you up, water you can drink, the light you're sitting in, a name in your phone you could call, each one coming into view like horses on a hillside.
Elisha, who prayed not for the army to vanish but for his frightened servant's eyes to open, and see the mountain full of chariots of fire.

776.title: Four lepers (2 Kings 7:3–9)
776.hook: outcasts find the enemy camp empty and decide to share the news
776.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the four lepers as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws for healing from skin disease in Leviticus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a servant's eyes were opened to a mountain full of chariots: more are with us. Today, Samaria is under siege and starving, and help comes from outside the gate.

Outside the gate of Samaria sit four men with a skin disease. The law keeps them outside the city, and the city is under siege by Aram, with famine inside. They do the math out loud: "Why sit we here until we die?" If we go into the city, there's famine, and we die there. If we sit here, we die here. So let's go over to the enemy camp. If they spare us, we live. If they kill us, we were dying anyway. At twilight, the four outcasts get up and walk toward the enemy.
screen: `FOUR MEN OUTSIDE THE GATE.` → `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: They reach the edge of the camp, and there's no one there. The Lord had made the army of Aram hear a noise of chariots and horses, the noise of a great host, and they fled in the twilight, leaving their tents, horses, donkeys, everything. So four hungry men walk into an empty camp full of food. They eat and drink in one tent, carry off silver, gold and clothing, and hide it. Then another tent. Who could blame them? And then they stop. One says: "We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace." These are the men the law kept outside the walls, and they're the ones who realize good news kept to yourself goes bad. They admit a plain worry, too: if we wait until morning light, some trouble will come upon us. So they go back in the dark and call to the gatekeepers: we came to the camp of Aram, and no one was there, only horses tied, and donkeys tied, and the tents as they were. The king suspects a trap. Scouts go out, find a trail of clothes and gear all the way to the Jordan. And the starving city walks out and eats. The good news came from the edge, from four people nobody expected to hear from. It reached the city because they decided a full stomach wasn't enough. A day of good tidings has to be told.
screen: `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` · `AN EMPTY CAMP FULL OF FOOD.` · then, large: `WE DO NOT WELL.` · then: `GOOD NEWS FROM THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what good thing you know that someone else doesn't: a job opening a friend could use, a thank-you you never passed on, praise you've said behind someone's back but never to their face. Let one come to mind, along with the person who needs it, and hold it ready, like the four men at the gate in the dark.
Four lepers. Outcasts at the gate of a starving city who found the enemy camp empty and decided they couldn't keep the news to themselves. Today's word.

777.title: The north falls (2 Kings 17)
777.hook: Assyria takes Samaria and the northern tribes are carried away and scattered
777.howItsDone: Jews read 2 Kings 17 as part of the Former Prophets, and the hope that the scattered tribes will one day be gathered appears in the prophets and in Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four outcasts at a city gate found an empty camp and said: this day is a day of good tidings. Today, the news runs the other way.

One chapter, and a kingdom ends. All week this path has been in the north, Israel, with its capital at Samaria. Elisha asked for pi shnayim, and his teacher's cloak fell to him. A woman in Shunem built a little room on her roof for a holy man. A proud general washed in the Jordan because a captive girl spoke up. A frightened servant had his eyes opened. Four lepers carried good news to a starving city. Today, in one chapter, that kingdom ends.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE NORTH.` → `CLOAK, ROOF, RIVER, GATE.` → `TODAY IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The last king of the north is named Hoshea. He stops paying tribute to Assyria and looks to Egypt for help. The king of Assyria marches in, besieges Samaria and takes it. He carries the people of Israel away into Assyria, and settles them in distant places the text names: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Then the chapter does something unusual. It stops telling the story and starts explaining it. The writer's answer is long and blunt: the people had turned to other gods, though the Lord had warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer: turn from your evil ways. They would not hear. And then one sad line: "there was none left but the tribe of Judah only." The king of Assyria brings people from other lands to live in the empty towns of Samaria. The map is redrawn. Those carried away never come back in the story; the book of Kings simply goes on with Judah. Later readers would call them the lost tribes, and tradition tells stories about where they went. But the prophets didn't let the north be forgotten. Ezekiel is told to take two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and join them into one in his hand. Jewish tradition keeps that hope alive: one day, the scattered come home. The lost tribes are lost to the record. They were not lost to memory.
screen: `HOSHEA TURNS TO EGYPT.` · `SAMARIA TAKEN, ISRAEL CARRIED AWAY.` · then, large: `NONE LEFT BUT THE TRIBE OF JUDAH.` · then: `THE STORY GOES SILENT.` · `TWO STICKS JOINED IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people whose names nobody wrote down: great-great-grandparents you can't name, a town that isn't on the map anymore, the workers who built a place you walk past every day. You don't need faces or details; with each slow breath, let one of them be real for a moment, people who cooked, worried, laughed, and were carried off by time. If you pray, you can remember them before God.
Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom, whose revolt against Assyria brought the siege that carried Israel away and ended the north.
Your line: the lost tribes. The north is gone from the story, not from the hope. Good to see you today.
